lessons.title: The Staple: Maize Meal Varieties
lessons.body: Maize meal is the foundation of sadza, ugali, nshima, and pap. In Africa, you'll find three main types: white maize meal (finely ground, used for sadza in Zimbabwe and nshima in Zambia), yellow maize meal (common in South Africa for pap, slightly sweeter), and whole grain maize meal (with germ and bran, more nutritious but coarser). For street food, white fine meal is most popular because it cooks smooth and looks clean. Buy from local mills or marketsâa 25kg bag of fine white maize meal costs about $15-$20 in most countries. Check for freshness: it should smell sweet, not musty. Store in a dry, airtight container away from sunlight. If you're in East Africa, ugali is usually made from white maize meal, but some vendors mix in cassava flour for a softer texture. In West Africa, they use fermented maize dough for banku and kenkey, but that's a different process. For this module, focus on the dry meal. You'll need a heavy-bottomed pot (at least 5 litres for a family-size batch), a wooden spoon or sturdy plastic spatula, and a whisk for smoothing lumps. A good pot costs $20-$30 and lasts years. Start with 1kg of meal to test your recipe. The ratio of meal to water is critical: for a stiff sadza, use 1 part meal to 3 parts water; for soft pap, 1 part meal to 4 parts water. Never guessâuse a measuring cup. Also, keep a separate small bowl of meal for dusting. Your first batch might be lumpy, but practice makes perfect. Remember, the staple is the cheapest part of the meal, so your profit margin is high if you cook it right.

lessons.title: Cooking Sadza and Ugali Perfectly
lessons.body: To cook perfect sadza or ugali, start by boiling water. For 1kg of maize meal, bring 3 litres of water to a rolling boil in a heavy pot. Add 1 tablespoon of salt. Now, the key step: mix 1 cup of maize meal with 1 cup of cold water to make a smooth paste (this prevents lumps). Slowly pour this paste into the boiling water, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon. Reduce heat to medium. The mixture will thicken. Now, add the remaining maize meal gradually, one handful at a time, stirring vigorously in one direction. This is the hard workâkeep stirring for 5-10 minutes until the mixture pulls away from the sides of the pot and forms a stiff ball. For ugali, you want a firmer consistency; for sadza, slightly softer. If it's too stiff, add a little hot water; if too soft, add a little meal. Cover and let steam on low heat for 5 minutes. Then stir again. The total cooking time is about 15-20 minutes. Test doneness: it should be smooth, not grainy. For street food, you can cook a large batch and keep it warm in a cooler box lined with a clean cloth. Serve with a wooden spoon or scoop. In Zimbabwe, sadza is served in a round mound; in Kenya, ugali is cut into slices. Practice making 5 batches to get consistent texture. Remember, undercooked sadza tastes raw and sticks to the teeth. Overcooked becomes rubbery. Use medium heat and constant stirring. A good trick: after cooking, invert the pot onto a plateâthe sadza should slide out in one piece. If it sticks, you didn't cook it enough. Sell within 4 hours for best quality.

lessons.title: Relish: Vegetable and Meat Stews
lessons.body: Relish is the sauce or stew that accompanies sadza. The most common is a tomato-onion base. For a basic vegetable relish, chop 2 onions, 4 tomatoes, and 1 green pepper. Heat 3 tablespoons of cooking oil in a pan. Fry onions until golden, add tomatoes and pepper, cook until soft. Add 1 cup of water, 1 teaspoon of salt, and 1 stock cube. Simmer for 10 minutes. You can add chopped cabbage, carrots, or green beans. For a meat relish, brown 500g of beef or chicken pieces in oil, then add the same tomato-onion base. Add 2 cups of water and simmer until meat is tender (beef takes 45 minutes, chicken 20 minutes). For a richer flavour, add 2 tablespoons of tomato paste. In many African countries, people add groundnut paste (peanut butter) to thicken and add proteinâ2 tablespoons stirred in at the end. Another popular relish is dried fish (kapenta) fried with onions and tomatoes. For street food, keep relish hot in a slow cooker or insulated container. Portion control: one ladle (about 100ml) per serving of sadza. Cost per serving: vegetable relish about $0.20, meat relish about $0.50. You can precook relish in large batches and reheat. Always taste and adjust salt. Avoid watery relishâit should coat the back of a spoon. If it's too thin, simmer uncovered to reduce. If too thick, add a little water. Common mistakes: burning onions (use medium heat), not cooking tomatoes long enough (they should break down), and under-salting. For a vegetarian option, use mushrooms or beans. Relish is where you can be creativeâadd spinach, pumpkin leaves, or even leftover meat. Just keep it saucy, not dry.

lessons.title: Muriwo, Covo and Leafy Greens
lessons.body: Leafy greens are the cheapest and most nutritious relish. Muriwo is the Shona word for leafy vegetables, typically rape (kale), covo (collard greens), or spinach. In East Africa, sukuma wiki (collard greens) is common. To prepare, wash leaves thoroughly in salted water to remove dirt and insects. Remove tough stems. Chop finely. For a classic muriwo, heat 2 tablespoons of oil in a pan, add 1 chopped onion and fry until soft. Add 2 chopped tomatoes and cook until mushy. Add the chopped greens and stir. Add 1/2 cup of water, 1 teaspoon of salt, and a pinch of baking soda (optional, keeps them green). Cover and steam for 5-8 minutes until tender but not mushy. For extra flavour, add 2 tablespoons of peanut butter or a splash of milk. In Zimbabwe, muriwo is often cooked with a bit of beef or chicken for flavour. For street food, you can cook greens in large batches and keep warm. They should be bright green, not dull. If they turn brown, you overcooked them. Portion: one serving is about 1/2 cup cooked greens. Cost: a bunch of covo costs $0.50 and serves 4. To reduce bitterness in covo, blanch in boiling water for 2 minutes, then drain before cooking. For a vegan version, skip the meat. For a richer version, add fried onions and tomatoes. Always taste before serving. Greens are a great way to add colour and nutrition to your plate. Pair with sadza and a protein. In many African markets, you can buy pre-washed and chopped greens, but they cost more. Buy whole bunches and prep yourself to save money. Store leftover cooked greens in the fridge for up to 2 days. Reheat with a little water to prevent drying.

lessons.title: Protein Sides: Beef, Chicken, Fish
lessons.body: Protein sides make your plate filling and profitable. The most common are beef, chicken, and fish. For beef, buy stewing beef (chuck or shin) because it's cheaper and becomes tender when slow-cooked. Cut into 2cm cubes. For 1kg beef, season with salt, pepper, and a pinch of curry powder. Brown in oil in batches, then set aside. In the same pot, fry onions, tomatoes, and garlic. Add the beef back, add 2 cups of water or stock, cover, and simmer for 1.5 to 2 hours until tender. For chicken, use thighs or drumsticksâthey stay juicy. Brown 1kg chicken pieces, then add the same tomato-onion base, 1 cup of water, and simmer for 30 minutes. For fish, tilapia or mackerel are affordable. Clean and scale, then fry in hot oil for 5 minutes per side. Or stew: fry onions and tomatoes, add 1 cup of water, then add fish and simmer for 10 minutes. In coastal areas, use dried fish like stockfish or catfish. For street food, keep proteins hot in a chafing dish or cooler. Portion control: 100g of meat per serving. Cost: beef $1.50 per serving, chicken $1.00, fish $0.80. To maximise profit, offer a small piece of meat with a lot of relish. You can also make meatballs or mince stew. Always cook meat thoroughlyâno pink inside. Use a meat thermometer if possible: beef 70Â°C, chicken 75Â°C. Store raw meat separately from cooked. Marinate chicken in lemon juice and garlic for 30 minutes to reduce smell. For beef, add a tablespoon of vinegar to tenderise. For fish, soak in milk for 10 minutes to remove fishiness. Serve hot. Never reheat meat more than once.

lessons.title: Plating and Portion Control
lessons.body: Plating is how you present your food to attract customers and control costs. For a standard plate of sadza and relish, use a round plate or a takeaway container. Place a scoop of sadza (about 200g cooked, the size of a tennis ball) in the centre. Flatten slightly with the back of a spoon. On one side, add 1 ladle (100ml) of relish. On the other side, add 100g of protein (meat, fish, or beans). If you have leafy greens, add 1/2 cup. The plate should look full but not overflowing. Use a colour contrast: white sadza, red tomato relish, green greens, brown meat. For takeaway, use a 3-compartment container: sadza in the large section, relish and protein in the smaller ones. Portion control is critical for profit. Weigh your sadza: 200g per serving. Use a measuring cup or scale. A 25kg bag of meal makes about 100 servings of 200g each. If you sell each plate for $2.50, your cost per plate is about $0.80 (meal $0.20, relish $0.20, protein $0.40). That's a 68% gross margin. But if you overserve, you lose money. Train your servers to use a standard ladle. For meat, count pieces: 3 pieces of chicken per plate. For fish, one medium tilapia. For beef, 5 cubes. Always serve with a smile. Keep your stall clean. Use gloves when handling food. Wrap sadza in cling film if not serving immediately. For events, pre-portion into containers. Offer a small discount for takeaway. Track your sales daily: how many plates sold, how much meal used. Adjust portions if you see waste. A good plate should satisfy an average adult. If customers complain about small portions, add more relish, not more sadza. Relish is cheaper. Remember, consistency builds trust. Use the same size scoop every time.

quiz.q: Which type of maize meal is most commonly used for sadza in Zimbabwe?
quiz.explanation: White fine maize meal is preferred for its smooth texture and clean appearance.

quiz.q: What is the ideal ratio of maize meal to water for stiff sadza?
options: A) 1 part meal to 2 parts water
B) 1 part meal to 3 parts water
C) 1 part meal to 4 parts water
D) 1 part meal to 5 parts water
quiz.explanation: A 1:3 ratio gives a firm, stiff sadza, while more water makes it softer.

quiz.q: Why do you mix a small amount of maize meal with cold water before adding to boiling water?
quiz.explanation: The cold water paste helps disperse the meal evenly, preventing lumps.

quiz.q: How long should you stir sadza after adding all the meal?
quiz.explanation: Constant stirring for 5-10 minutes develops the smooth texture and cooks out raw taste.

quiz.q: What is a sign that sadza is properly cooked?
options: A) It sticks to the pot
B) It pulls away from the sides of the pot
D) It has a raw smell
quiz.explanation: When cooked, sadza forms a ball and pulls away from the pot's sides.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common ingredient in a basic vegetable relish?
quiz.explanation: Onions and tomatoes form the base of most African relishes.

quiz.q: What can you add to a relish to thicken it and add protein?
quiz.explanation: Groundnut paste thickens the relish and adds a rich, nutty protein.

quiz.q: How long does beef take to become tender when simmered in a relish?
quiz.explanation: Stewing beef requires long, slow cooking to break down connective tissue.

quiz.q: What is muriwo?
options: A) A type of maize meal
B) A leafy green vegetable relish
quiz.explanation: Muriwo is the Shona word for leafy greens, often cooked as a relish.

quiz.q: How can you keep leafy greens bright green when cooking?
options: A) Add a pinch of baking soda
quiz.explanation: A small amount of baking soda helps retain the green colour.

quiz.q: What is covo?
quiz.explanation: Covo is a common leafy green, similar to collard greens, used in relishes.

quiz.q: How do you reduce bitterness in covo before cooking?
options: B) Blanch in boiling water for 2 minutes
quiz.explanation: Blanching removes some of the bitter compounds.

quiz.q: Which protein is usually the cheapest per serving?
quiz.explanation: Fish like tilapia or mackerel is often the most affordable protein.

quiz.q: What is a good way to tenderise beef before cooking?
quiz.explanation: Acidic ingredients like vinegar help break down tough fibres.

quiz.q: How long should you marinate chicken in lemon juice and garlic to reduce smell?
quiz.explanation: 30 minutes is enough to neutralise odours without overpowering the chicken.

quiz.q: What is the recommended internal temperature for cooked chicken?
quiz.explanation: Chicken must reach 75Â°C to ensure harmful bacteria are killed.

quiz.q: How many grams of cooked sadza is a standard serving?
quiz.explanation: 200g is a typical portion that satisfies an average adult.

quiz.q: What is a good way to control portion sizes for profit?
options: A) Use a standard ladle or scale
B) Serve as much as possible
quiz.explanation: Standard measures ensure consistency and prevent overserving.

quiz.q: Which of these is a colour contrast that makes a plate attractive?
options: A) White sadza, red relish, green greens
quiz.explanation: Varied colours make the meal visually appealing.

quiz.q: What is the approximate cost per serving of vegetable relish?
quiz.explanation: Vegetable relish is inexpensive, around $0.20 per serving.

quiz.q: How can you keep cooked sadza warm for service?
options: A) In a cooler box lined with a cloth
quiz.explanation: A cooler box retains heat and keeps sadza soft.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when cooking sadza?
quiz.explanation: Insufficient stirring leads to lumps and uneven texture.

quiz.q: Which leafy green is commonly used in East Africa for sukuma wiki?
quiz.explanation: Sukuma wiki is typically made from collard greens.

quiz.q: What is a good way to add flavour to leafy greens without meat?
quiz.explanation: Peanut butter adds richness and protein to vegetarian greens.

quiz.q: How should you store raw meat?
options: D) In a cool box with vegetables
quiz.explanation: Separate storage prevents cross-contamination.

quiz.q: What is a sign that oil is hot enough for frying fish?
options: B) It bubbles when a small piece of fish is added
quiz.explanation: Bubbling indicates the oil is hot enough to fry without absorbing too much oil.

quiz.q: How many pieces of chicken are typically served per plate in street food?
quiz.explanation: Three pieces provide a satisfying portion without overserving.

quiz.q: What is a good practice for food safety when serving?
quiz.explanation: Gloves prevent contamination from hands.

quiz.q: Why is it important to track daily sales and meal usage?
options: A) To know when to raise prices
B) To control portions and reduce waste
quiz.explanation: Tracking helps identify waste and adjust portion sizes for profit.

quiz.q: What should you do if customers complain about small portions?
quiz.explanation: Relish is cheaper than sadza, so adding more relish satisfies without high cost.
